subject: cfa() function - how fast should it run?

messages.author: 2df5ffb4cf5ba603
messages.subject: cfa() function - how fast should it run?
parts:
I have a factor structure with 7 latent factors and 50 variables that I want to run through cfa() with a dataset, where the dataset contains around 3000 rows. 

When I do this, the function takes ~10-11 seconds to complete, which is very, very slow. Does this sound normal for the cfa() function?

messages.author: 89c9fc822e34b78c
messages.subject: Re: cfa() function - how fast should it run?
parts:
On 03/16/2015 05:42 AM, Zachary Nevin wrote:
> I have a factor structure with 7 latent factors and 50 variables that I
> want to run through cfa() with a dataset, where the dataset contains
> around 3000 rows.
>
> When I do this, the function takes ~10-11 seconds to complete, which is
> very, very slow. Does this sound normal for the cfa() function?

Yes. There are a few reasons why lavaan (in general) is relatively slow
(compared to say LISREL or Mplus):

1) lavaan is (currently, 0.5-17) written 100% in R; there is no compiled
code

2) the lavaan/cfa/sem/growth functions are simply not designed to be
speedy; they are designed to be convenient, full-of-information, and
user-friendly

3) the lavaan/cfa/sem/growth functions compute a lot of additional
statistics that you may not need, but they are (sometimes) used by
add-on packages. One example is the 'Gamma' matrix (the asymptotic
variance matrix of the sample statistics), which is always computed when
estimator = "ML", even if you do not need it.

4) at several places, lavaan checks if a matrix is positive definite, by
computing the eigenvalues explicitly; especially for the Gamma matrix,
this becomes a very time-consuming operation if the number of variables
goes up

One day, I may provide a cfa.light() function, that is designed for
speed. In addition, future updates will give the user more access to the
lower-level functions, so you can assemble your own 'sem()' function,
doing only what you need.

Yves.
